boston-roxbury-grant-lawsuit-2026.excerpt: The city says the U.S. Department of Transportation unlawfully withdrew a 2022 award for safety, transit and accessibility work on three major corridors.
boston-roxbury-grant-lawsuit-2026.text: boston sues over $20m grant for roxbury street upgrades the city says the u.s. department of transportation unlawfully withdrew a 2022 award for safety, transit and accessibility work on three major corridors. the city of boston has gone to federal court to recover a $20 million transportation grant that officials say was withdrawn after the project included a small electric-vehicle charging component. the lawsuit, filed sept. 28 in the u.s. district court for the district of massachusetts, asks the court to reverse the u.s. department of transportation's cancellation of the 2022 award for the roxbury resilient corridors project. the filing and case number, city of boston v. duffy, are listed in the public docket record (https://dockets.justia.com/docket/massachusetts/madce/1:2026cv14419/306825). the dispute centers on three roxbury streets: melnea cass boulevard, malcolm x boulevard and warren street. boston's project page says the grant was intended to support street repairs, safer crossings, transit improvements, accessibility work, traffic-flow changes, trees, lighting, public spaces and stormwater features. the city describes the corridors as central roadways in a historically disinvested neighborhood and says the project was being developed with local residents and community organizations (https://www.boston.gov/departments/transportation/project/roxbury-resilient-corridors). according to a sept. 28 announcement from u.s. rep. ayanna pressley and mayor michelle wu, the city argues that dot cited the project's electric-vehicle charging infrastructure as the reason for canceling the entire award. the announcement says that charging work represented less than 1% of project costs and that federal transportation officials had previously encouraged the city to include it. those are the city's allegations about the cancellation; the lawsuit has not produced a merits ruling (https://pressley.house.gov/2026/09/28/pressley-wu-announce-lawsuit-against-trump-administration-to-protect-20-million-federal-grant-for-roxburys-street-improvements/). the guardian independently reported that the case names transportation secretary sean duffy and was filed against the department over its decision to withdraw the money. the newspaper also reported the city's position that federal agencies cannot rewrite a program established by congress to match changing political priorities. the department's response was not included in the sources reviewed for this report, so the federal government's legal defense and any timetable for responding remain unclear (https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/28/boston-sues-trump-administration). the stakes are practical for people who use roxbury's busiest routes. boston says the project is meant to improve bus service, walking, bicycling and driving conditions at the same time. on its warren street project page, the city says more than 20,250 mbta riders use that corridor each weekday and that delays can add as much as 20 minutes to an average rider's day. that page predates the lawsuit and describes the broader transit problem rather than measuring the effect of the canceled grant, but it helps explain why the city treats the award as more than a budget line (https://content.boston.gov/departments/transportation/project/warren-street-bus-priority-corridor). roxbury's transportation history also shapes the argument. boston says the wide, vehicle-oriented corridors were created through eminent-domain and block-clearance decisions during the urban-renewal era of the 1960s. the city's current plan calls for safer crossings, more comfortable bus stops, shade and cooling spaces, bike infrastructure and green stormwater measures, while also trying to prevent displacement and support small businesses. those goals remain proposed project features, not completed improvements. the case arrives after the city had already approved accepting the federal award. a boston city council record from april 2025 describes the $20 million raise grant as funding to reconstruct and upgrade the three roxbury corridors. the city now says the cancellation removed a major share of the money needed to move the work forward. whether the court restores the award, sends the decision back to dot for reconsideration or leaves the cancellation in place will determine what boston can realistically build and when (https://content.boston.gov/departments/city-council/city-council-roll-call-votes?page=39). for now, the lawsuit is an opening filing, not a ruling that boston has won or that dot acted unlawfully. the public docket shows the case was assigned to u.s. district judge richard g. stearns after an initial judge recused himself on the filing date. the next meaningful developments will be the federal defendants' response, any request for interim relief and the court's decision on how the administrative procedure act claims proceed. until then, the three-corridor project remains listed by boston as pending, with its completion year undetermined. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma boston roxbury, boston massachusetts boston roxbury transportation federal grants public transit infrastructure

ct-bottle-deposit-law-penalties-2026-10-.excerpt: A new statute bars people from collecting Connecticut refunds on containers bought elsewhere and allows misdemeanor or felony charges when the volume reaches thousands of bottles or cans.
ct-bottle-deposit-law-penalties-2026-10-.text: connecticut bottle-deposit law adds criminal penalties for large out-of-state redemptions a new statute bars people from collecting connecticut refunds on containers bought elsewhere and allows misdemeanor or felony charges when the volume reaches thousands of bottles or cans. connecticut's latest bottle-deposit changes took effect oct. 1, adding criminal penalties to the state's effort to stop people from redeeming large quantities of beverage containers that were purchased somewhere else. [public act 26-148](https://www.cga.ct.gov/2026/act/pa/pdf/2026pa-00148-r00sb-00457-pa.pdf) says no person may collect or charge a refund value on a container not purchased in connecticut, and it applies to conduct the law describes as willful. the statute sets escalating criminal categories by volume. willfully redeeming 5,000 to 19,999 out-of-state containers in a calendar year is a class b misdemeanor under the act. the law identifies 20,000 to 30,999 containers during a one-year period as a class a misdemeanor, and 40,000 or more as a class d felony. the published act does not state a separate threshold in the text between 31,000 and 39,999 containers, an omission that could matter if prosecutors try to apply the new scale to a case in that range. the law is aimed at a problem that grew after connecticut raised its standard deposit from five cents to 10 cents in january 2024. connecticut is one of a small group of states with bottle-return programs, while neighboring rhode island has no cash-deposit system and new york generally uses a five-cent deposit. that difference can create an incentive to bring containers across a state line and collect connecticut's higher refund, even though the deposit was never paid here. [ct insider](https://www.ctinsider.com/connecticut/article/bottle-deposit-law-changes-october-1-22441604.php) reported oct. 3 that connecticut's redemption rate rose sharply after the 10-cent deposit began, then declined as other controls took effect. the [connecticut department of energy and environmental protection](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/reduce-reuse-recycle/bottles/connecticut-bottle-bill) reported an 85.7% rate for the first quarter of 2026 and 79.6% for the quarter ending june 30, according to the report. those figures show how many containers were redeemed, but they do not identify how many returns were fraudulent or how many came from outside the state. the new criminal provision is one part of a broader regulatory response. [deep's bottle-bill guidance](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/reduce-reuse-recycle/bottles/connecticut-bottle-bill) says redemption-center owners and operators must obtain a state license beginning july 1, 2026, and submit a $2,500 fee with the application. earlier changes also created identification and record-keeping requirements for high-volume returns and set daily limits. the rules are designed to give the state more information about who is redeeming containers and how much material passes through each center, although enforcement still requires investigators to connect a person to a large number of containers and show that the conduct was willful. the law specifically exempts common or contract carriers and warehouse workers who are lawfully transporting or storing beverage containers as merchandise, along with employees acting within that job. that language distinguishes ordinary shipping and distribution from the conduct the statute targets. it also means the new penalties are not a blanket ban on moving beverage containers across state lines; the issue is collecting connecticut's refund on containers that were not bought in connecticut. the dispute has consequences beyond people waiting in redemption-center lines. [ct insider](https://www.ctinsider.com/connecticut/article/bottle-deposit-law-changes-october-1-22441604.php) described beverage distributors as absorbing handling and refund costs when redemption volumes exceed the number of containers sold in the state. a bridgeport redemption-center owner told the publication that new scanning equipment could change how quickly his employees process returns and could affect staffing. connecticut's challenge is to reduce cross-border abuse without making legitimate recycling harder for consumers, charities and businesses that depend on the deposit system. [deep](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/reduce-reuse-recycle/bottles/connecticut-bottle-bill) has said the bottle bill remains an environmental program as well as a financial one: deposits are intended to keep containers out of roads, waterways and landfills and to feed usable material back into manufacturing. the oct. 1 law therefore starts another phase of a policy experiment that connecticut began when it doubled the deposit. state officials will have to see whether licensing, identification, scanning and the new criminal thresholds stabilize redemption rates without shifting too much cost onto redemption centers or ordinary residents. connecticut connecticut connecticut ct hartford connecticut connecticut bottle bill recycling environmental policy consumer protection

ct-fall-turkey-firearms-season-2026-10-0.excerpt: The season runs Oct. 3 through Oct. 31, while a new state rule clarifies when small-game and turkey hunters need landowner permission.
ct-fall-turkey-firearms-season-2026-10-0.text: connecticut fall firearms turkey season opens with updated permission rules the season runs oct. 3 through oct. 31, while a new state rule clarifies when small-game and turkey hunters need landowner permission. connecticut’s fall firearms turkey season opens saturday, oct. 3, and runs through oct. 31, the department of energy and environmental protection announced friday. the opening applies to eligible state and private lands, while the state’s pheasant and broader small-game seasons are scheduled to begin oct. 17. fall archery seasons for deer and turkey began sept. 15, giving connecticut hunters several overlapping ways to use the state’s forests and private landscapes this month. [deep’s opening notice](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/news-releases/news-releases---2026/deep-announces-opening-days-of-fall-turkey-pheasant-and-small-game-hunting-seasons) describes the firearms opener as part of the agency’s annual schedule and urges hunters to participate safely and responsibly. the basic turkey rules are specific. the fall firearms bag limit is three turkeys of either sex on private land, state land or a combination of the two. hunting hours begin one-half hour before sunrise and end at sunset. connecticut residents need a firearms hunting license and a resident game bird conservation stamp. nonresidents need either a three-day out-of-state bird-hunting license or a nonresident firearms license, along with the stamp. the state’s [2026 wild-turkey guide](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/hunting/2026-connecticut-hunting-and-trapping-guide/wild-turkey-hunting) says shotguns must be 20 gauge or larger, use no. 4 through no. 7 1/2 shot or a permitted combination, and be limited to three shells. access rules matter as much as the season dates. a hunter on private land must carry signed written consent from the landowner on deep’s official form for the current season. turkey hunting is allowed on sundays only on private land, and sunday hunting cannot take place within 40 yards of a blazed public trail. hunters using state land should check deep’s interactive hunting-area map because not every state property is open to fall firearms turkey hunting. decoys are allowed, but live decoys are prohibited. the 2026 season also arrives with a permission change that took effect oct. 1. deep says verbal permission is sufficient for small-game hunting on private land every day of the week, including sundays. deer and turkey hunters still need written permission from private landowners. the agency also says the legal definition of a muzzleloader has changed: the projectile must be loaded from the muzzle end. those distinctions are important for people moving between small-game, deer and turkey seasons, because permission requirements do not apply identically to each activity. deep’s safety guidance focuses on preventing a person from being mistaken for a bird. hunters should remain in a fixed location and call turkeys to them rather than stalk a turkey or a turkey call. before firing, they should identify the target and what lies beyond it. the guide recommends sitting with protection from an approaching hunter, such as a tree at least as wide as the hunter’s shoulders, and placing a four- to six-inch fluorescent-orange band around the tree about six feet above the ground to identify the calling position. hunters should not wear red, white, blue or black while turkey hunting, and deep recommends fluorescent orange while walking to and from the hunting area and when carrying a harvested bird. harvest paperwork continues after a successful hunt. a hunter must immediately complete and sign a harvest tag and keep it with the turkey until the carcass is cut up for consumption. deep also requires deer and turkey harvests to be reported within 24 hours through its online hunter reporting website or by calling 1-877-337-4868, according to the agency’s [fall archery season notice](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/news-releases/news-releases---2026/fall-archery-deer-and-turkey-season-opens-in-september). the reporting requirement gives wildlife managers information for monitoring harvest and managing connecticut’s turkey population. for people sharing the woods, the opening changes the mix of activity on public properties beginning this weekend. hikers and other visitors should pay attention to posted notices and avoid entering closed or restricted areas, while hunters need to confirm the property rules before setting up. deep’s guide includes the season dates, license requirements, map links and landowner forms in one place. the next major statewide opening is oct. 17, when pheasant and several small-game seasons begin; closing dates vary by species. new-england new-england new england ct connecticut connecticut hunting season wild turkey outdoor safety deep

ct-i91-windsor-ejection-2026-10-01.excerpt: A person was taken to Hartford Hospital with serious injuries after being ejected in a two-car crash that closed southbound I-91 in Windsor Thursday evening.
ct-i91-windsor-ejection-2026-10-01.text: person seriously injured after ejection in windsor i-91 crash a person was taken to hartford hospital with serious injuries after being ejected in a two-car crash that closed southbound i-91 in windsor thursday evening. one person was seriously injured thursday evening after being thrown from a vehicle in a two-car crash on interstate 91 south in windsor, connecticut state police said. the collision closed a section of the highway during the evening commute and remained under investigation overnight. connecticut department of transportation officials said the crash was reported at about 5:15 p.m. between exits 36 and 35b. the agency reported the southbound closure while state police and emergency crews worked at the scene. the reported closure covered both a windsor interchange and the adjoining southbound segment, making the incident a significant travel disruption for drivers using the corridor. state police told the connecticut post that the person ejected from the vehicle was taken to hartford hospital by windsor emergency medical services with serious injuries. authorities did not release the person's name, age or condition beyond that description. they also did not identify the other driver or disclose whether anyone else was hurt. multiple state police units responded, according to the connecticut post's account of the investigation. the newspaper reported that the scene was still active around 9:15 p.m., several hours after the crash was first reported. police had not announced a cause, and the available reports did not say whether speed, impairment, weather, a medical event or another factor played a role. those possibilities remain unconfirmed and should not be treated as explanations. the transportation disruption continued into the night. the connecticut post reported heavy traffic near the closure at about 9:23 p.m., citing the department of transportation. patch later reported that the highway reopened late thursday night. the closure limits reported by ctdot were the same in both accounts: southbound i-91 between exits 36 and 35b. patch reported early friday that windsor ems transported the injured person to hartford hospital and that connecticut state police were investigating. patch also noted that the reports did not identify the person or explain what caused the crash. wfsb, which first reported the closure, separately described the incident as a two-vehicle crash and attributed the road information to ctdot and the serious-injury information to state police. for windsor and neighboring communities, the immediate concern was the combination of a serious injury scene and a highway shutdown during a busy travel period. the reopening restored the route, but it did not resolve the questions surrounding the collision. any later police statement could clarify the sequence of impact, the vehicles involved and whether additional charges or citations are warranted. state police had not announced further details by early friday. until investigators release more information, the confirmed account is limited: a two-vehicle crash occurred on southbound i-91 in windsor, one person was ejected and seriously injured, windsor ems took that person to hartford hospital, and the highway was closed and later reopened. sources: [connecticut post](https://www.ctpost.com/journalinquirer/article/windsor-i-91-south-closed-crash-thursday-22458805.php), [patch](https://patch.com/connecticut/windsor/person-seriously-injured-i-91-crash-windsor), and [wfsb](https://www.wfsb.com/2026/10/01/i-91-south-closed-windsor-after-crash/). new-england new-england new england ct windsor windsor, connecticut connecticut windsor i-91 traffic connecticut state police ctdot

ct-kosta-diamantis-sentenced-2026-09-30.excerpt: Kosta Diamantis was sentenced in absentia for extortion, bribery and false-statement convictions tied to school-construction contracts; federal authorities are still seeking him.
ct-kosta-diamantis-sentenced-2026-09-30.text: former connecticut official sentenced to 7 years after fleeing to greece kosta diamantis was sentenced in absentia for extortion, bribery and false-statement convictions tied to school-construction contracts; federal authorities are still seeking him. former connecticut school-construction official konstantinos “kosta” diamantis was sentenced wednesday to 84 months in federal prison and three years of supervised release, but he was not in the bridgeport courtroom to hear the punishment. the 70-year-old former state official had fled to greece before sentencing, and the u.s. attorney’s office for the district of connecticut said law enforcement is seeking him. the federal announcement is at https://www.justice.gov/usao-ct/pr/former-state-official-sentenced-7-years-federal-prison-school-construction-extortion-and. u.s. district judge stefan r. underhill imposed the sentence for convictions involving extortion, bribery, conspiracy and false statements. a federal jury in bridgeport found diamantis guilty in october 2025 on 21 counts: two counts of extortion, two extortion-conspiracy counts, two bribery counts, two bribery-conspiracy counts and 13 counts of making false statements to federal agents, according to the justice department. connecticut public reported that the case grew out of diamantis’s work as the state’s former deputy budget director and director of the office of school construction grants and review. that office administered grants for connecticut public-school construction projects seeking state funding. prosecutors said diamantis used the position to demand and receive payments from contractors while helping them obtain or preserve work. the justice department identified projects involving a school project in tolland, state reimbursement work for new britain and renovations at hartford’s bulkeley high school. the release says one contractor paid diamantis with cash and checks and hired his daughter at an inflated salary; those details describe the conduct underlying the convictions, not new untested allegations. the sentence came after an unusual break in the normal criminal-justice process. diamantis had been scheduled to appear for sentencing in september but did not attend. ct mirror reported that his lawyer told the court diamantis had left the united states and was in greece, where he holds dual citizenship. the later sentencing could proceed without him, but his absence leaves the practical question of how and when he will be taken into custody. federal officials have not announced that he has returned to the united states. the financial consequences are not settled. the justice department said judge underhill will determine restitution after additional court proceedings. that decision could identify losses that the government says were caused by the scheme, but the sentencing announcement did not give a final restitution amount. the unresolved figure matters because the projects at issue involved public school construction and state reimbursement, placing the case's consequences beyond the contractors and former official who appeared in court. the prison term was also shorter than the range sought by prosecutors. ct mirror reported that the government recommended a guideline range of 121 to 151 months, while the judge imposed 84 months. the difference does not change the convictions or the three-year supervised-release term, but it will be part of the record as prosecutors pursue diamantis and the court addresses restitution. ct mirror’s sentencing report is at https://ctmirror.org/2026/09/30/kosta-diamantis-still-a-fugitive-sentenced-to-84-months/. the case is not finished for the other people involved in the investigation. the justice department said contractors identified as duffy, monarca and roy pleaded guilty to related charges and are awaiting sentencing. the investigation was conducted by the fbi and irs criminal investigation, and federal prosecutors said the bribery scheme involved multimillion-dollar school-construction projects. connecticut public’s account of the sentencing, including the fact that diamantis remained outside the country, is at https://www.ctpublic.org/news/2026-09-30/kosta-diamantis-cts-disgraced-former-deputy-budget-director-sentenced. for connecticut, the public-interest question now extends from the sentence to the systems that allowed a senior official overseeing school-building money to steer contractors while concealing conduct from investigators. the court has established criminal responsibility through the jury’s verdict and the sentence; it has not yet completed restitution proceedings or resolved diamantis’s custody. those next steps will determine how much money is recovered, whether the former official is returned to face the prison term and what accountability reaches the related contractors. new-england new-england new england ct bridgeport bridgeport, connecticut connecticut kosta diamantis public corruption school construction bribery federal court

ct-leap-attendance-grants-2026-09-30.excerpt: The new grants expand a home-visiting program that state officials say helped drive four straight years of lower chronic absenteeism, but the latest awards will still have to translate into local services.
ct-leap-attendance-grants-2026-09-30.text: connecticut awards $6.2m to 29 districts to improve student attendance the new grants expand a home-visiting program that state officials say helped drive four straight years of lower chronic absenteeism, but the latest awards will still have to translate into local services. connecticut is awarding approximately $6.2 million to 29 school districts and regional education organizations for a home-visiting program aimed at bringing chronically absent students back into regular contact with their schools. the grants, announced sept. 30 by gov. ned lamont and education commissioner charlene russell-tucker, are being distributed through the learner engagement and attendance program, known as leap. the money comes from a $7 million state budget line item. about $800,000 will support statewide infrastructure such as home-visitor training, program implementation and data collection, according to the [connecticut governor’s announcement](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/09-2026/governor-lamont-and-commissioner-russell-tucker-announce-state-grants-to-expand-program). leap pairs trained school staff and community partners with students and families. the visits are intended to identify the practical or personal barriers behind missed school days and connect families with services that can make regular attendance possible. the program began in 2021 with federal pandemic-relief money, initially serving 15 districts. it later expanded to 25, and this round brings the state’s reach to 29 districts for the 2026-27 school year. the recipients include some of connecticut’s largest districts. waterbury is slated to receive $525,000, hartford $500,000, bridgeport $475,000 and new haven $425,000. stamford will receive $350,000, while smaller awards go to districts including east windsor, east haven, plainfield and jamestown. middletown’s $125,000 award was reported separately by [middletown patch](https://patch.com/connecticut/middletown-ct/middletown-school-system-getting-6-figure-grant-aimed-boosting-attendance), which described the grant as funding for the same statewide leap effort. state officials say connecticut’s chronic-absenteeism rate fell from 23.7% in the 2021-22 school year to 16.4% in 2025-26. the governor’s office calculated that change as nearly 35,000 more students attending school regularly than at the earlier point. the figures describe statewide movement and do not establish that leap alone caused the decline; the announcement calls the program one part of a broader attendance strategy. there is earlier research behind the state’s decision to continue the program. the center for connecticut education research collaboration, a partnership involving the state education department and connecticut colleges, studied leap’s first 15 districts. its [published evaluation](https://portal.ct.gov/ccerc/current-projects/leap) found attendance gains after home visits, including an average increase of nearly 15 percentage points six months after visits for students served during the 2021-22 school year. the study also reported different effects by grade level and district, which matters because the new grant round includes a broader mix of communities than the initial cohort. connecticut says home visitors have conducted about 88,000 visits and reached roughly 53,000 students since leap began. those totals are cumulative program figures supplied by the state, not an independent count released with the new awards. the current announcement also does not provide a district-by-district attendance target or a deadline for demonstrating results. the immediate test will be local execution. districts will need to recruit or assign visitors, train them, coordinate with community organizations and turn conversations with families into help with transportation, health, housing, counseling or other barriers when those needs are identified. if the grants produce lasting attendance gains, connecticut will have a stronger case for making the home-visiting model a durable part of school operations after the pandemic-era funding that launched it has faded. new-england new-england new england ct hartford connecticut connecticut student attendance chronic absenteeism leap public schools education funding

ct-middletown-veterans-cemetery-expansio.excerpt: A $584,250 federal grant, paired with $294,250 in state money, will help Connecticut expand its only state-operated veterans cemetery as cremation burial space nears capacity.
ct-middletown-veterans-cemetery-expansio.text: middletown veterans cemetery expansion will add 1,510 cremation plots a $584,250 federal grant, paired with $294,250 in state money, will help connecticut expand its only state-operated veterans cemetery as cremation burial space nears capacity. connecticut will expand the state veterans cemetery in middletown with 1,510 new burial plots for cremated remains, state officials announced friday. the project will use a $584,250 grant from the u.s. department of veterans affairs alongside $294,250 that connecticut has already allocated, adding capacity at a cemetery that serves veterans and eligible family members from across the state. the [governor’s announcement](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/10-2026/governor-lamont-announces-funding-to-expand-the-connecticut-state-veterans-cemetery-in-middletown) was also covered locally by [middletown patch](https://patch.com/connecticut/middletown-ct/middletown-veterans-cemetery-expansion-add-cremation-burial-plots). the work is planned for a parcel next to the existing cemetery at 317 bow lane. the property was formerly used by connecticut valley hospital and was recently transferred from the state department of mental health and addiction services to the department of veterans affairs, which is overseeing the expansion. the location allows the state to extend an existing cemetery rather than wait for a separate site to be developed. under the state’s announcement, the federal money will pay for the cremains burial plots and related site work, including an entrance gate, fencing, landscaping, irrigation components, concrete-block storage bays, site furnishings and supporting infrastructure. the state funding will support demolition of cottage 22, a vacant connecticut valley hospital building on the property. connecticut has not announced a completion date for the construction. the expansion is aimed at a specific capacity problem. the [connecticut department of veterans affairs](https://portal.ct.gov/dva/cemetery-and-memorial-services) says the middletown cemetery currently has 14,718 burial plots and 3,000 columbarium niches. state officials estimate that the existing supply of in-ground cremation plots will be exhausted around january 2028 without additional space; with the expansion, those plots are projected to remain available through at least december 2033. that timing matters because the cemetery offers several distinct choices for families. the project concerns in-ground burial of cremated remains, while casket burials and above-ground columbarium niches are separate options. the state says extending the cremation-plot supply through 2033 would bring the estimated depletion dates for all three options into alignment, giving officials time to plan a future cemetery intended to serve veterans and their families over the longer term. the middletown site was established in 1985 and is the largest state-operated veterans cemetery in connecticut, according to the department of veterans affairs. the department’s [cemetery-services page](https://portal.ct.gov/dva/cemetery-and-memorial-services) says the site is the final resting place for more than 16,000 veterans and family members. connecticut also maintains the colonel raymond f. gates cemetery in rocky hill, which is reserved primarily for veterans residing at the state’s residential and skilled-nursing facilities, and provides perpetual care for spring grove veterans cemetery in darien, which is closed to new burials. the funding announcement follows a longer state effort to secure land and keep the middletown facility eligible for federal cemetery support. a [2023 state bond authorization](https://portal.ct.gov/-/media/opm/bud-capital-budget/agendas/cy-2023/agenda%5fdec15%5f2023.pdf) set aside $3 million for land acquisition and improvements connected to the department of veterans affairs cemetery program. a subsequent state planning document said the middletown cemetery was expected to approach capacity within several years, while an [environmental scoping notice](https://portal.ct.gov/ceq/das/scoping-notice/dva-cemetery-expansion) identified the bow lane expansion area and estimated that existing space could be depleted in about 4.6 years. for connecticut veterans’ families, the immediate result is a planned increase in local burial capacity, not a new benefit or completed construction project. the state and federal awards still have to be translated into demolition, site preparation and cemetery improvements. the announcement does not specify the construction schedule or the final operating date for the new plots. the department of veterans affairs will remain responsible for project oversight and for coordinating burial services while the expansion proceeds. connecticut veterans veterans ct middletown middletown, connecticut connecticut middletown veterans cemeteries department of veterans affairs

ct-recreational-trails-grants-2026-10-01.excerpt: The grants will support construction, accessibility work, planning and maintenance, with half of the selected projects serving distressed municipalities or environmental-justice communities.
ct-recreational-trails-grants-2026-10-01.text: connecticut awards $10.5m for 50 recreational-trail projects the grants will support construction, accessibility work, planning and maintenance, with half of the selected projects serving distressed municipalities or environmental-justice communities. connecticut is awarding approximately $10.5 million to 50 projects intended to build, repair, connect and improve recreational trails across the state, gov. ned lamont and the department of energy and environmental protection announced thursday. the awards come through the connecticut recreational trails grant program after a competitive review by deep and the connecticut greenways council. the money was previously allocated by the state bond commission, according to the [governor’s announcement](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/10-2026/governor-lamont-announces-state-grants-for-recreational-trails). the program supports more than new stretches of pavement: the 2026 list includes construction, rehabilitation, bridge replacement, accessibility upgrades, trailhead and parking improvements, planning and design, equipment, outreach and long-term maintenance. that mix means the award will produce different kinds of results in different communities. winchester received $749,000 for construction intended to complete the sue grossman still river greenway. new haven received $274,730 for planning and design at the east rock park college woods inclusive community trail, while naugatuck received $400,000 to design a connector for the naugatuck river greenway between naugatuck and waterbury. bridgeport received $180,000 for planning and design of the old mill green pathways project, and east hartford received $200,000 to design a gap closure on the east coast greenway. the geographic spread is one reason the grants matter beyond individual trailheads. other awards include $505,000 for a multi-use connector in avon, $495,000 for an accessible bridge and trail at steep rock association’s hidden valley preserve, $492,874 for the university of connecticut’s trails and active-living program, and $498,400 for the connecticut forest and park association’s blue-blazed trail system and woodland conservation corps. the full award table also includes projects in eastern connecticut, the shoreline, the hartford region and the northwest hills. twenty-five of the 50 projects are in, or serve, municipalities the state classifies as distressed or environmental-justice communities. that designation does not mean every project has the same scope or construction schedule, but it signals that the review process gave weight to communities that have not always had equal access to outdoor recreation. the state says the awards are designed to improve public access while supporting recreation, active transportation, conservation and local connections. there is already evidence of substantial demand for the network. connecticut’s trail census, a uconn program that uses infrared counters and volunteer-supported data collection, recorded more than 2.7 million trail uses at 27 monitored locations during 2025, the state release said. the [uconn ct trails program](https://cttrails.uconn.edu/) maintains the census and a public trail-finder system; its 2025 count report is listed in the program’s [research archive](https://cttrails.uconn.edu/pubs/reports/). counter totals measure recorded uses at monitored sites, not every trip on every trail, so they should be read as an indicator rather than a statewide attendance total. the program also arrives as connecticut continues to treat trails as public-health and economic infrastructure. deep describes more than 2,000 miles of multi-use trails in state parks and forests alone, while the governor’s office said outdoor recreation contributes about $6 billion annually to the state economy and supports more than 50,000 jobs. those figures come from state and federal economic accounts cited in the announcement, not from an independent assessment of this grant round. the next phase will be local implementation. planning awards still require design work, permits and decisions about routes, access and maintenance before construction can begin. construction awards will need to be matched with contracting, scheduling and long-term upkeep. for residents, the practical question is when each town or organization can turn its award into a safer crossing, a more accessible trail, a completed connection or a maintained public route. the grant list provides the funding commitments; project timelines will depend on the recipients and the state’s agreement process. new-england new-england new england ct hartford connecticut connecticut ct-suffield-school-bus-crash-2026-10-01.excerpt: A Region 12 bus carrying students left South Grand Street and struck a building Thursday morning; police said the cause remains under investigation.
ct-suffield-school-bus-crash-2026-10-01.text: suffield school bus crash sends 11 to hospitals with minor injuries a region 12 bus carrying students left south grand street and struck a building thursday morning; police said the cause remains under investigation. eleven people were taken to two local hospitals with minor injuries thursday after a small school bus carrying students left the roadway and struck a building in suffield, connecticut. the crash brought police, fire and ambulance crews to south grand street and left investigators working to determine why the bus veered off the road. suffield police said officers responded to the area of 425 south grand st. at about 9:49 a.m. after receiving a report of a motor-vehicle crash with possible injuries. their preliminary account said the bus was traveling north toward mountain road when it left the right shoulder and collided with a building beside the street. police did not announce a mechanical problem, medical event, weather factor or other cause. the bus came from regional school district 12, which serves communities in the shepaug valley. nbc connecticut reported that students were aboard, while the suffield volunteer ambulance association said 15 people, including the driver, were on the small bus. the association said 10 students and the driver were transported for evaluation. authorities did not release the students’ ages or identify the hospitals. the ambulance response required help from several nearby agencies. the ambulance association said it sent three ambulances staffed by paramedics, while enfield ems and the windsor locks lions club ambulance provided additional units. north central cmed helped coordinate the transports and contacted receiving hospitals to confirm that they could accommodate the patients. that coordination also shaped how the students were handled after the crash. according to the ambulance association’s statement reported by patch, responders tried to keep the students together when possible so school staff and families could receive information more easily. region 12 personnel came to the scene to assist the students, and emergency officials said the response was managed through the area’s normal mutual-aid system. the ambulance association also pushed back on online descriptions of the incident as a mass-casualty or multi-casualty event. it said the scene required significant coordination but did not meet that designation. that distinction describes the emergency-management classification, not the seriousness of the reported injuries: police and ambulance officials said everyone taken for treatment had minor injuries. hearst connecticut media reported that the bus was carrying shepaug valley school students on the way to a fair and that a region 12 official said the vehicle was driven by a properly licensed teacher. that account adds context to the trip but does not resolve the central unanswered question of what caused the bus to leave south grand street. police interviewed people involved and said the investigation was continuing. south grand street was closed while the scene was investigated and later reopened, according to local reports. no charges or citations had been announced in the available accounts. for families and residents, the immediate outcome was that the 11 people transported for care had reported minor injuries; the longer-term questions concern the crash sequence, the condition of the building and any findings by police or the school district. sources: [suffield police department details reported by patch](https://patch.com/connecticut/suffield/crash-reported-south-grand-street-suffield), [nbc connecticut](https://www.nbcconnecticut.com/news/local/11-people-sent-to-hospitals-after-school-bus-crashes-into-building-in-suffield/3780574/), [wfsb](https://www.wfsb.com/2026/10/01/school-bus-crashes-into-building-suffield-police-confirm/), and [hearst connecticut media](https://www.stamfordadvocate.com/journalinquirer/article/region-12-school-bus-crash-suffield-ct-south-grand-22457938.php). new-england new-england new england ct suffield suffield, connecticut ct-uconn-blue-emergency-phones-injunctio.excerpt: A judge declined to issue an immediate shutdown order but set an Oct. 9 hearing on a parent’s request to keep the campus emergency phones operating while the dispute proceeds.
ct-uconn-blue-emergency-phones-injunctio.text: uconn parent asks court to halt storrs blue-light phone removals a judge declined to issue an immediate shutdown order but set an oct. 9 hearing on a parent’s request to keep the campus emergency phones operating while the dispute proceeds. a parent of a university of connecticut student is asking a state court to pause the university’s removal of blue-light emergency phones from the storrs campus, opening a new legal fight over whether a physical emergency network can be retired as cellphones and safety apps become more common. the court declined to grant an immediate, before-hearing injunction, but scheduled a remote preliminary hearing for oct. 9 at 9:30 a.m., according to reporting by [nbc connecticut](https://www.nbcconnecticut.com/news/local/uconn-parent-sues-school-to-stop-removal-of-blue-light-emergency-phones/3780793/) and [hearst connecticut media](https://www.newstimes.com/news/education/article/uconn-blue-emergency-phones-lawsuit-22457637.php). billyjoe contreras filed the application oct. 1 in connecticut superior court, citing concerns about campus safety. his request would bar uconn from disconnecting, disabling, removing or decommissioning the existing blue-light phones and associated safety lights at storrs while the case is pending. he also asks the university to continue maintaining and operating the system. the immediate request was an ex parte application, meaning contreras sought temporary relief before a full hearing with the university; the judge’s decision leaves the phaseout dispute open rather than deciding whether the phones must ultimately remain. in an affidavit described by hearst, contreras argues that a student’s personal phone may be unavailable, uncharged, lost, stolen or unusable during an emergency. his filing says removing a nearby fixed device without an equivalent replacement could create a gap in access to help. that is an allegation and safety argument from the plaintiff, not a court finding. the oct. 9 proceeding is expected to give the parties a chance to discuss whether they can resolve the issue; if they cannot, the court may schedule a later evidentiary hearing. uconn has defended the phaseout as a technology and cost decision. nbc connecticut reported that the university says it received only two legitimate blue-phone calls in the past five years: one reporting a car crash and another from someone who believed they were being followed, a concern the university said was unfounded. the school told nbc that modernizing the system would cost about $6 million and that annual operating expenses exceed $70,000 as aging equipment requires more repairs. the university is not planning to remove every phone. uconn has said it will keep devices in locations where cellular coverage is weaker and is assessing which sites meet that test. for other students, the school points to personal cellphone calls, text-to-911 and the livesafe app, which can connect users to the university’s emergency communications center by text, video or phone. students interviewed by nbc said those tools do not entirely replace a clearly marked device that can be activated without finding or unlocking a personal phone. uconn’s own [division of university safety page](https://police.universitysafety.uconn.edu/emergency-blue-phones/) describes the existing storrs system as a network of phones located throughout campus: a user presses a button, describes the emergency to a dispatcher and a police officer is sent to the location. that design matters to the dispute because the devices serve students, employees and visitors who may not have a working phone immediately available. the university’s current public description explains how the system operates, but it does not establish how many storrs phones will remain after the review. the question of usage is still developing. a sept. 28 entry in [uconn’s public-records log](https://publicrecords.uconn.edu/requests/fpo-26-639-09-28-26-819-am/) shows an open request seeking the number of emergency blue phones at storrs as of aug. 31, the largest number ever installed and a year-by-year count of calls over the prior 25 calendar years. those records could add context to the university’s five-year figures, but the request itself is not a response from the school and does not yet provide the requested data. the next legal milestone is the oct. 9 remote hearing. until then, the court has not ordered uconn to stop its work, and the university’s plan to retain some phones in weak-service areas remains the stated approach. the case will turn on evidence about the remaining devices, their reliability and use, the alternatives available at each location and the practical safety consequences of removing them. for the storrs community, the immediate issue is not whether cellphones are widespread; it is whether that coverage is sufficient at every place and moment where a person may need help. new-england new-england new england ct storrs storrs, connecticut connecticut uconn storrs campus safety emergency phones higher education courts

ct-yale-tony-reno-death-2026-10-02.excerpt: Reno led Yale to five Ivy League championships and 83 wins during a 14-year tenure that reshaped the Bulldogs’ place in the FCS.
ct-yale-tony-reno-death-2026-10-02.text: former yale football coach tony reno dies at 52 reno led yale to five ivy league championships and 83 wins during a 14-year tenure that reshaped the bulldogs’ place in the fcs. tony reno, the former yale football coach who guided the bulldogs through five ivy league championships, has died at 52, yale athletics announced friday. the news reached the new haven campus less than eight months after reno stepped down from the program for health reasons. the [yale memorial](https://yalebulldogs.com/news/2026/10/2/in-memoriam-former-football-head-coach-tony-reno.aspx) described a coach whose influence extended beyond wins and losses into the lives of the students he mentored. the associated press, in [reporting carried by the boston globe](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/10/02/sports/reno-yale-football/), said no cause of death was given. reno’s record places him among the most successful coaches in yale’s long football history. he went 83-49 over 14 seasons, according to yale and the ap, and ranks second in career victories behind carm cozza. his teams won ivy league titles in 2017, 2019, 2022, 2023 and 2025. yale also beat harvard in seven of the final nine meetings under reno, giving his tenure a particularly strong mark in the rivalry that anchors the program’s season each fall. the final championship season added a new chapter. yale’s official account of reno’s tenure says the 2025 bulldogs finished 8-2 in the regular season and 6-1 in league play, earning the ivy league’s first automatic berth in the ncaa football championship subdivision playoffs. yale then rallied from a 28-point deficit to beat youngstown state 43-42 in the opening round before losing 21-13 to eventual national champion montana state. the bulldogs finished no. 13 in the final fcs rankings. that run gave the program a national stage while preserving the ivy league’s academic and athletic identity. reno left the job in february, when he said his health situation made stepping down the right decision for yale football. in its [announcement at the time](https://yalebulldogs.com/news/2026/2/17/tony-reno-steps-down-as-head-coach-of-yale-football.aspx), the university said reno had led the program since january 2012 and had helped establish a foundation for the next coach. he had spent more than a decade on yale’s staff before becoming head coach, including work under jack siedlecki on the 2006 ivy championship team. kevin cahill took over the program after a national search. the numbers tell only part of why the announcement is significant to yale and the region. yale said six bulldogs won the asa s. bushnell cup as ivy league player of the year during reno’s tenure, while five yale players were selected in the nfl draft over the past seven years covered by the university’s february review. the school also credited reno’s teams with success in the classroom and community. in its memorial, yale emphasized his standards for student-athletes and the relationships he built with players, colleagues and alumni rather than presenting the coaching change simply as a succession story. reno’s connection to the area ran through both new haven and massachusetts. yale identified him as a massachusetts native, and the university’s account of his career says he spent his early yale years as an assistant before returning to lead the bulldogs. his family remained part of the program’s public story: the ap reported that he is survived by his wife, toni, and their children, dante, angelina and vince. dante was yale’s quarterback during the 2025 championship season, when the bulldogs made their first fcs postseason appearance. for yale, the immediate task is continuing a program that reno left with a conference title, a playoff win and a clear competitive identity. for new haven, his death closes the chapter on a coach who spent much of his career tied to the city and its university. yale’s tribute makes clear what will be measured now: not only how the bulldogs perform under cahill, but how much of reno’s emphasis on mentorship survives in the players who follow him. new-england new-england new england ct new haven new haven, connecticut connecticut new haven yale college football ivy league tony reno

ma-blandford-wildlife-corridor-2026-10-0.excerpt: The new public conservation land links more than 39,000 acres across the Mass. Pike while adding habitat and outdoor recreation space in western Massachusetts.
ma-blandford-wildlife-corridor-2026-10-0.text: massachusetts protects 580 acres in blandford wildlife corridor the new public conservation land links more than 39,000 acres across the mass. pike while adding habitat and outdoor recreation space in western massachusetts. massachusetts conservation agencies and the nature conservancy have completed a project protecting more than 580 acres in blandford, creating new public land on both sides of interstate 90 and strengthening a wildlife connection through the western massachusetts hills. the [massachusetts executive office of energy and environmental affairs](https://www.mass.gov/news/healey-driscoll-administration-protects-over-580-acres-for-wildlife-and-outdoor-recreation-in-blandford) announced the project oct. 2. [western mass news](https://www.westernmassnews.com/2026/10/03/more-land-added-chester-blandford-stare-forest/) independently reported the same acreage and the new designations. the protected property is divided into a 360-acre masswildlife blandford wildlife management area and a 218-acre addition to chester-blandford state forest. the former christmas tree farm crosses the mass. pike and connects more than 39,000 acres of already protected land, according to state officials and the local report. that makes the project more than a stand-alone open-space purchase: it closes a gap in a larger landscape where animals can move between habitat on opposite sides of one of new england's busiest highways. the land is open to the public for outdoor recreation, although the announcement did not provide a separate trail map, parking plan or operating schedule for the new management area. residents and visitors will need to rely on updates from masswildlife and the department of conservation and recreation for practical access information as management details are posted. the property contains mature and young forest, agricultural grasslands, wetlands and four brooks: sanderson, cushman, finley and peebles. those waterways are part of the westfield river watershed. state agencies said the conservation work will help protect water quality and nearby drinking-water supplies, while preserving cold-water fish habitat used by species such as eastern brook trout. the corridor also has a direct transportation-safety dimension. the state says masswildlife, dcr, massdot and the nature conservancy have been working to understand how animals cross roads and highways. at the blandford site, massdot and the nature conservancy are monitoring a culvert under i-90, where black bears, bobcats, coyotes, river otters and other wildlife have been documented passing through, according to the state announcement. keeping that route connected can help animals reach food, water and seasonal habitat while giving planners evidence for future crossing improvements. the project includes habitat that can support the new england cottontail, massachusetts' only native rabbit, which state officials describe as vulnerable to habitat loss. protecting connected forest and grassland does not guarantee that the rabbit or any other species will expand here, but it preserves the kind of varied landscape wildlife managers say is necessary for movement and adaptation as conditions change. blandford's acquisition is part of a broader state conservation strategy. massachusetts' biodiversity goals call for doubling the pace of land and water protection, with targets of conserving 30 percent by 2030 and 40 percent by 2050. the administration said its proposed mass ready act includes $304.5 million for land-protection programs and $20 million tied to biodiversity goals; those are proposed investments, not funds this project alone received. for the hilltowns, the immediate result is a permanently protected stretch of forest, streams and open land that can serve both residents and wildlife. the agencies involved still have to translate the acquisition into day-to-day public access and long-term habitat management. the new designations give them the protected footprint; future agency plans will determine how visitors use it and how the corridor is monitored over time. massachusetts environment environment ma blandford blandford, massachusetts massachusetts blandford conservation wildlife outdoor recreation

ma-college-closure-risk-notice-2026-10-0.excerpt: Higher-education officials are planning an earlier public-warning deadline for financially distressed private colleges after two Massachusetts schools announced plans to close last spring.
ma-college-closure-risk-notice-2026-10-0.text: massachusetts colleges may have to disclose closure risk by dec. 31 higher-education officials are planning an earlier public-warning deadline for financially distressed private colleges after two massachusetts schools announced plans to close last spring. massachusetts higher-education officials are planning to require private colleges and universities judged to be at risk of imminent closure to post a public notice by dec. 31, an effort to give students, employees and surrounding communities more time to respond to a financial crisis. the proposed timing was described by outgoing department of higher education commissioner noe ortega during the board of higher education's sept. 29 meeting, according to wbur and the state house news service (https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/09/30/massachusetts-private-colleges-higher-ed-closing-risk-schools). the change would not mean that every school posting a notice is certain to shut down. under the state's financial assessment and risk monitoring, or farm, system, an institution is considered at risk of imminent closure when the commissioner determines that it may be unable to continue operations or substantially meet its obligations to enrolled and admitted students through the current and following academic year. the massachusetts department of higher education says the system is intended to identify risks, monitor mitigation plans and reduce disruption to students, families, faculty, staff and host communities (https://www.mass.edu/strategic/farm.asp). the state already requires colleges to alert the board of higher education about known financial liabilities or risks that could lead to an imminent closure or prevent the institution from fulfilling its obligations. the department's farm materials say those immediate notifications are confidential, while public notice is part of a later process if the institution's financial condition remains sufficiently uncertain after review and risk-mitigation planning. the department also requires private institutions to post annual financial reports and plain-language summaries on their websites. the proposed dec. 31 date is meant to make the public-warning process more predictable. wbur reported that current regulations use dec. 1 as the annual threshold measurement date for deciding whether a college can meet its obligations for the rest of the current academic year and the next one, while the board currently has flexibility about when after that date to make a determination. board chairman chris gabrieli said a december determination would reduce the risk that students and staff learn about a potential closure only after they have made plans for the spring semester. the discussion follows two massachusetts closures announced near the end of the last academic year. anna maria college in paxton and hampshire college in amherst cited financial difficulties in announcing plans to close, wbur reported. hampshire's public notice from the department of higher education says the college planned to end academic programming at the end of 2026 while continuing academic programs, residential support and transition services for enrolled students through dec. 31 (https://www.mass.edu/strategic/documents/2026-04-14-hampshire-noitce-posting-for-dhe-website.pdf). the notice also says the department could not confirm that hampshire had enough resources to sustain current operations and fulfill obligations through the current and subsequent academic years; that is a regulatory finding, not a claim that every massachusetts college faces the same condition. massachusetts has been building this oversight system since the sudden 2018 closure of mount ida college. the department says 24 colleges and universities closed, merged or began winding down between 2014 and 2022, and that the 2019 farm law and later regulations were designed to improve financial monitoring and closure planning. those rules can require a contingency plan covering student deposits and records, and in some cases a bond or letter of credit to help protect those obligations. the department's current process describes screening from november through april, review of risk-mitigation plans from june through october, and determinations and contingency planning in november and december. officials also said the board plans to add staff and use outside firms to strengthen financial assessments, while revising required training for private-college trustees. the goal, gabrieli said, is to give students time to identify transfer options, give faculty and staff a reasonable period to seek other work, and reduce the shock to communities that depend on a campus. the timing matters this fall because ortega's term as commissioner ended sept. 30 and josé luis santos began serving as interim commissioner on oct. 1, according to the department (https://www.mass.edu/). the public-warning deadline remains a planned policy change rather than a newly announced closure list. the next questions are whether the board of higher education formally adopts the dec. 31 timetable, which institutions are identified through the annual farm review, and what mitigation or teach-out plans follow. until those steps occur, students should not read the proposed deadline as evidence that a particular college is about to close; it is an attempt to move information earlier when the state does determine that a school's finances may threaten its ability to serve students. massachusetts massachusetts
